svg.title: What the runner does with an ack, a nack, a retry and a dead-letter
svg.desc: Two parts. Above, the settlement sequence between broker, driver source, runner, handler and the dead-letter destination. Below, the decision the runner takes when a handler returns an error: the directive the error carries is read first, then the ordering mode decides how the next attempt happens, then the attempt bound decides whether the failure policy applies. The dead-letter route publishes and confirms BEFORE it acks the original, and a publication it cannot confirm requeues the original rather than acking it.
svg.text: PART A · THE SETTLEMENT SEQUENCE
Fetch(ctx, dst)
bounded: len(dst) is the prefetch, never a callback
the client library's own poll / receive / long poll
records, and the broker's own delivery count where it keeps one
[]DriverDelivery
Attempt = the broker's count, or 0 where it keeps none
handler(ctx, d)
one serial worker per assigned lane by default; a panic is recovered into *PanicError and retried
return nil
d.Ack()
the ONLY positive settlement: the runner never acks a handler that returned an error
return err
→ PART B decides what this becomes
The dead-letter order is the whole point
1. dlq.Publish(copy + provenance headers)
2. confirmed → d.Ack()
refused / ambiguous → requeue, count, NEVER ack
An ambiguous dead-letter publication may duplicate in the dead-letter topic. That is the chosen direction: §4.2 already makes a duplicate
something a consumer handles, and a poison message nobody can recover is not. The provenance headers are
iqmq-origin-topic · iqmq-origin-subscription · iqmq-attempts · iqmq-failure · iqmq-first-delivered-at
— and the last is written only when this delivery IS the first, because a redelivery may reach a different process and nothing in the SPI
carries a first-delivery time back. A missing header says "not known"; one holding this attempt's receive time would say something false.
On a driver whose broker moves the message itself (WithNativeDeadLetter) there is no publication and no window — and no provenance headers,
because nothing on that path writes a message: the destination receives what the broker put there.
PART B · WHAT A FAILED DELIVERY BECOMES
DirectiveOf(err)
read first, before any backoff

g.text: the handler's decision, logged and counted, never silent and never the runner's
in that order: the fetch stops before the record is redeliverable, so the runner
cannot hand itself the same message on its way out. The requeue is synchronous, so nothing is lost.
without exhausting the attempts. With NO dead-letter destination it HALTS:
dropping the message instead is the one answer §4.5 forbids.
a directive replaces the DELAY and never the attempt bound. Default: bounded
exponential jittered backoff, five attempts by default.

svg.text: How the next attempt happens — §4.4's ordering mode, not the error
OrderingRelaxed
(default) give it back: Nack(NackDelay(d)). Traffic behind it carries on.
OrderingStrict
hold the lane here and call the handler again: nothing overtakes it, and the
attempts become exact even on a broker that counts none — at the price of a worker parked for the backoff.
OrderingStopOnFailure
Out of attempts → the failure policy
FailureHalt
(default without a DLQ) *PoisonError, requeue
FailureDeadLetter
(default WITH one) PART A
FailureSkip
acks a message nobody handled — never a default
The bound can be unreachable, and knowing when matters more than the diagram:
a broker that keeps NO delivery count reports Attempt = 0, and a message this runner gave back carries nothing else — so under the default
relaxed ordering the runner can never call it exhausted, and it is retried for as long as it keeps failing. Strict ordering, or a broker with a native
count, makes the bound real. The capability matrix says which drivers count attempts.
Read with run.go's fail / retry / exhaust / deadLetter. Every arrow above is one of those functions.
